title: RNA structures regulate norovirus life cycle and enable rational attenuation in vivo.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and parsed 4 of 8 GEO files (all four ShapeMapper 2.2 reactivity profiles) plus one .map file: each is 7,382 rows (one row per nucleotide of the 7,382-nt murine norovirus CW3 genome), 47-50 columns, gzipped tab-separated, read by pandas on the first try. Non-missing normalized reactivity: 7,313 / 7,303 (SHAPE 2A3 replicates 1/2) and 7,271 / 7,307 (fbDMS replicates). Measured replicate agreement myself: Pearson r = 0.970 between SHAPE replicates, 0.788 between fbDMS replicates, ~0.38 across reagents. Median sequencing depth 34,000-48,000 reads per nucleotide; only 57 nucleotides below 5,000. Also downloaded from the authors' GitHub: both secondary-structure CT files (7,382 rows each, 57.0% and 56.8% of nucleotides paired, 96.0% agreement on paired-versus-unpaired state between replicates) and two alignments (49 pan-norovirus and 18 murine norovirus ORF1 sequences, 5,061 aligned columns). Ran two positive controls on the files: DMS reactivity is highest at A and C and lowest at G (medians 0.581 / 0.328 / 0.119), and nucleotides unpaired in the structure model are ~3x more reactive than paired ones (SHAPE medians 0.455 versus 0.159). Total download 1.9 MB.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: That ShapeMapper 2.2 and SuperFold were used with a 500-nt maximum base-pair distance; that probing was in BV2 murine microglial cells at multiplicity of infection 0.05 for 24 h; the mutant-virus and mouse-infection phenotypes (plaque titres, genome copies, weight loss), which appear only in figures and were not downloaded; the Ribonanza dataset size (~2 million sequences), which I read in search results and did not download. Europe PMC's supplementary-file endpoint returned a non-zip response, so the four supplementary tables (primers, alignment accessions, locked nucleic acid designs, mutant plasmid sequences) were read only as captions in the PubMed Central XML.

a1_downloadable.note: GEO series GSE310315 is public; I fetched five files over plain HTTPS with no login, and the GitHub repository named in the data-availability statement is public and complete.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: The label is the existing column 'Norm_profile' (normalized per-nucleotide chemical reactivity), with 'Norm_stderr' beside it. No construction needed. Caveat: the paper's other interesting outcome, the fitness effect of disrupting a structure, is NOT a column - it exists only as plaque titres in figures for 13 mutant viruses.

a3_inputs_present.note: Each row carries its own base in the 'Sequence' column, and the full reference genome FASTA (murine norovirus CW3, GenBank EF014462.1) is in the GitHub repository. No identifier lookups required.

a4_units_stated.note: Reactivity is a unitless normalized ratio produced by ShapeMapper 2.2's standard box-plot normalization; the methods name the tool and version, and every raw ingredient (mutation counts, read depth, mutation rate) is present so the value can be recomputed. Marginal pass: the unit convention comes from the tool's documentation, not from a units column in the file.

a5_enough_rows.note: 7,313 nucleotides carry a normalized SHAPE reactivity value (I counted). LOUD CAVEAT: these rows all come from one RNA molecule in one cell line, so the number of independent biological units is one, not 7,313. Rows pass the literal threshold; the effective sample size does not support training a model, only testing one.

a6_fits_laptop.note: All four reactivity profiles plus both structure files and the alignments total 1.9 MB downloaded; the whole analysis is a few megabytes in memory.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: All four profiles have exactly 7,382 rows, matching the murine norovirus CW3 reference genome length and the '7382 ConsensusModel' header of both CT structure files. No disagreement anywhere.

a8_label_provenance.note: Reactivity is a direct chemical measurement: a reagent (2A3 or dimethyl sulfate) modifies flexible or unpaired bases, the modification is read out as a mutation during reverse transcription, and the rate is compared with an untreated control - all three count columns are in the file. CIRCULARITY WARNING for a different task: the CT secondary-structure files are SuperFold output computed FROM these same reactivities, so predicting the structure while using reactivity as a feature would be leakage by construction.

B1.why: Four flat tables, each keyed on an integer nucleotide position 1-7382; the join is exact and trivial (checked).

B2.why: Gzipped tab-separated, parsed first try, but has duplicated and blank trailing header names from ShapeMapper's appended histogram block.

B3.why: Authors already normalized ('Norm_profile'); one lab, one cell line, one pipeline version, so profiles are directly comparable.

B4.why: No censored or qualitative values; 69 of 7,382 nucleotides are blank at low depth and drop trivially (counted).

B5.why: Nucleotide position is unique 1-7382 in every file; no duplicate rows (checked).

B6.why: ShapeMapper 2.2 column names are documented by the tool; methods state version and parameters; readme files in the repository.

C1.why: Transfer question ('does a sequence-only reactivity model work in cells?') is informative either way, but one genome makes the answer anecdotal.

C2.why: RibonanzaNet has open weights and was trained on the same two reagents at far larger scale, but never tested on long in-cell viral RNA.

C3.why: Angle is diversity/unique application (in-cell, full-length, viral), but this paper contributes a single genome to it.

C4.why: In-cell probing of a whole viral genome is months of wet-lab work: infection, two reagents, two replicates, amplicon libraries, deep sequencing.

C5.why: RibonanzaNet is runnable as a published baseline; I already computed the dummy (per-base median reactivity) from the files.

D1.why: RibonanzaNet and RNA-FM are open-weight RNA models on GitHub/HuggingFace and take exactly this input, raw RNA sequence.

D2.why: Windowed CPU inference over 7,382 nucleotides is cheap, but there is no second genome to train a head on.

D3.why: Both backbones are publicly distributed, but I did not open either licence file in this evaluation.

E1.why: No leakage-free split: neighbouring nucleotides share structure, and all data come from one molecule.

E2.why: At most six holdable groups (three open reading frames, VF1, two untranslated regions), all from the same genome.

E3.why: Per-base median dummy computed from the files: SHAPE medians A 0.009, C 0.242, G 0.228, U 0.925.

E4.why: Measured noise floor: replicate Pearson r = 0.970 (SHAPE) and 0.788 (fbDMS), plus a per-nucleotide standard-error column.

E5.why: Two controls verified in the files: dimethyl sulfate reactive at A/C not G, and unpaired bases ~3x more reactive.

E6.why: Label shuffling and base-identity ablation are one line each on a 7,382-row table.

E7.why: Second reagent (fbDMS) is orthogonal in-house; published in-cell probing of other viral genomes exists, though I did not download it.

E8.why: The paper reports no prediction-accuracy number; RibonanzaNet's published scores are on its own short-construct test set.

G1.why: Identifiers are a GenBank accession (EF014462.1) plus nucleotide coordinate; standard, but cross-virus joins need sequence alignment.

G2.why: Named partners: the Ribonanza chemical-mapping dataset and the RNA Mapping Database, joinable on RNA sequence.

G3.why: Within-genome key is clean one-to-one; aligning this genome to other viruses' probing data is manageable but not automatic.

G4.why: Combined question: do reactivity models trained on short in-vitro RNA hold up on long RNA probed inside cells?

H1.why: Reactivity is continuous and reported genome-wide, so both reactive and unreactive nucleotides are systematically present (verified distribution).

H2.why: One virus strain, one cell line (BV2 microglia), one time point, one lab - stated in the paper and the GEO record.

H3.why: The honest claim can be written precisely in one sentence (see honest_claim_h3).

H4.why: The paper has an explicit 'Limitations of the study' section naming the generalizability gap to human norovirus.

I1.why: Named users: the Pyle lab (Yale), the Das lab / Eterna-RibonanzaNet community, and virology groups designing structure-targeting antisense oligos.

I2.why: A clear transfer failure would tell probing labs not to trust in-silico reactivity in cells, but one genome is thin evidence.

I3.why: Per-nucleotide correlation is roughly right, but the real decision is which 40-nt element to target, an element-level call.

I4.why: Base identity alone explains a lot (verified per-base medians) and thermodynamic folding is a strong simple baseline.

J1.why: Mostly zero-shot inference and evaluation plumbing; no training set means little real model fitting.

J2.why: Sanity checks are textbook and I already ran two of them successfully on the files.

J3.why: Shareable at every stage: the strong per-base reactivity skew I found (SHAPE median A 0.009 versus U 0.925) is a note on its own.

J4.why: Roughly one to two weeks, but not a number committed anywhere.

J5.why: No kill date or condition written down.

existing_models.name: RibonanzaNet (deep network predicting per-nucleotide chemical reactivity from RNA sequence, Das lab / Stanford)
existing_models.score_and_split: Trained on chemical-mapping measurements for roughly two million RNA sequences using the same two reagents as this paper (2A3 for SHAPE, dimethyl sulfate for DMS); evaluated on held-out short synthetic constructs from the Kaggle Ribonanza competition, not on long RNA probed inside cells. I read this from search results and the model card, and did not rerun it.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Generalization beyond the short, mostly in-vitro constructs the training library contains - long natural RNAs and the in-cell context are named as open.

existing_models.name: RNA-FM (RNA foundation model, self-supervised on ~23 million non-coding RNA sequences)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported as the strongest single-sequence RNA language model across structure and function benchmarks; a 2025 Briefings in Bioinformatics benchmark of RNA language models found their advantage largely disappears out of distribution, and all methods scored below 0.15 on the longest-sequence family. Read from search results only.

existing_models.name: RiNALMo (general-purpose RNA language model)
existing_models.score_and_split: Published in Nature Communications 2025 as generalizing well on secondary-structure prediction tasks; splits are RNA-family based, not viral in-cell data. Read from search results only.

existing_models.name: SuperFold with RNAstructure (thermodynamic folding constrained by experimental reactivity) - the method the authors themselves used
existing_models.score_and_split: No accuracy number is reported here; it produced the consensus structure model (57.0% of nucleotides paired, replicates agreeing on paired state at 96.0%, both counted by me from the CT files).
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Whether the modelled structures are functionally conserved in human norovirus; whether structure-guided attenuation transfers.

backbone.name: RibonanzaNet (primary; predicts 2A3 and dimethyl sulfate reactivity from sequence) with RNA-FM as an embedding alternative
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU is enough for windowed inference over 7,382 nucleotides (minutes), but freeze-and-head training is not viable because there is only one genome to fit a head on.
backbone.licence: Both are publicly distributed on GitHub/HuggingFace; I did not open either licence file, so treat terms as unverified.

integration.partner_dataset: The Ribonanza chemical-mapping dataset (~2 million RNA sequences probed with the same 2A3 and dimethyl sulfate reagents) and the RNA Mapping Database, plus published in-cell genome-wide probing of other RNA viruses (SARS-CoV-2, HIV-1, dengue).
integration.join_key: RNA sequence itself, or nucleotide coordinate within a reference accession (here GenBank EF014462.1).
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does a reactivity predictor trained on short, mostly in-vitro RNA constructs still work on long RNA probed inside living infected cells, and if not, does the error grow with distance from the training distribution (length, in-cell protein coating, genome region)?

controls.positive_control: Two, both already verified on the files: dimethyl sulfate reactivity must be high at A and C and low at G (measured medians 0.581, 0.328, 0.119), and nucleotides called unpaired in the authors' structure model must be clearly more reactive than paired ones (measured SHAPE medians 0.455 versus 0.159).
controls.negative_control: Shuffle the reactivity labels and confirm collapse to the per-base median dummy; ablate base identity to see how much of any prediction is just 'U is reactive, A is not'.
controls.external_validation: The orthogonal fbDMS reagent profiles in the same deposit (cross-reagent Pearson r = 0.38, measured), and published in-cell probing of other viral genomes, which I did not download.

honest_claim_h3: On a single 7,382-nucleotide murine norovirus CW3 genome probed in BV2 mouse microglial cells 24 h after infection, a sequence-only reactivity predictor trained on short in-vitro RNA constructs achieves per-nucleotide correlation X with measured in-cell 2A3 reactivity, which is Y relative to the trivial per-base-median baseline - a statement about one genome, one cell line and one time point, not about viral RNA in general.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a viral RNA genome's sequence to predict how chemically reactive each of its bases is inside infected cells.
plain_idea.train_on: There is no training set in this paper: the model would be trained elsewhere (the Ribonanza collection of chemical-mapping measurements on roughly two million RNA sequences) and only tested here. This deposit provides 7,313 labelled nucleotides (verified count) from one genome.
plain_idea.predict: A reactivity value per nucleotide. The true answer is a direct chemical measurement: the reagent 2A3 (or dimethyl sulfate) sticks to bases that are flexible or unpaired, that modification is converted into a mutation during reverse transcription, and the mutation rate is compared with an untreated control.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Labs that design antisense drugs against RNA viruses currently need months of wet-lab probing per genome; knowing whether a free sequence-only predictor matches in-cell measurements tells them whether that work can be skipped. Even a clear failure is useful, because it marks in-cell probing as irreplaceable.

more_or_better_data.why: This deposit is one genome with 7,313 labelled nucleotides; RibonanzaNet was trained on chemical-mapping data for about two million sequences using the same two reagents. Our only edge is the setting (full-length viral RNA probed inside cells), not the volume.

confidence_score.why: Two biological replicates per reagent and a per-nucleotide standard-error column let us state the measurement noise floor (replicate Pearson r = 0.970 for SHAPE, 0.788 for fbDMS, both measured by me), which bounds any model's achievable accuracy - but the Ribonanza data also carries replicate error, so this is not a unique capability.

models_beatable.why: RibonanzaNet (2024) is a convolution-plus-transformer network trained on ~2 million sequences, and RiNALMo is 2025; with one genome we cannot train a competitor at all, only run theirs and report where it fails.

guaranteed_improvement.why: The condition 'our model sees everything theirs sees plus the new data' fails outright: with one genome there is no 'our model' to train, and no shared evaluation split exists.

label_elsewhere.sources: Ribonanza (2A3 and dimethyl sulfate reactivity for roughly two million RNA sequences, Das lab, open - found by search, not downloaded); the RNA Mapping Database and RASP, which aggregate chemical-probing profiles (known resources); published genome-wide in-cell probing of SARS-CoV-2, HIV-1 and dengue (known literature).
label_elsewhere.join_key: RNA sequence, or nucleotide coordinate within a reference accession (GenBank EF014462.1 here)
label_elsewhere.why: The same measurement exists at vastly larger scale elsewhere, which means this genome's best role is as a held-out in-cell test case rather than as training data.

ambitious.why: Publishes RNA structure methods and benchmarks; would need a cross-virus in-cell benchmark of five or more probed genomes showing a specific, characterized failure mode of sequence-only reactivity models, not a single-genome figure.

realistic.why: Publishes short benchmark and re-evaluation notes; a careful zero-shot test of RibonanzaNet and RNA-FM on this one in-cell viral genome against a per-base-median baseline is exactly that size of result.

fallback.journal: bioRxiv preprint plus a machine-learning-in-computational-biology workshop
fallback.why: Even a negative result ('the predictor does no better than knowing the base identity on long in-cell RNA') plus the per-base reactivity skew observation is worth posting, and costs little.

pitch.headline: A whole 7,382-nucleotide virus genome's chemical structure map, measured inside infected cells by two reagents, two replicates, 1.9 MB total.
pitch.what_makes_the_data_unusual: Verified in the files: two orthogonal reagents, replicate agreement of 0.970 (SHAPE) and 0.788 (fbDMS), median depth above 34,000 reads per base, and an author-built structure model whose replicates agree 96% on paired state.
pitch.the_win: A number like 'RibonanzaNet reaches per-nucleotide Spearman 0.4 against in-cell 2A3 reactivity, versus 0.3 for a per-base-median baseline and a 0.97 replicate ceiling' - the first honest in-cell, full-length-genome score for that model.
pitch.even_if_it_fails: You learn the measurement ceiling (replicate r = 0.970) and that base identity alone carries much of the signal: verified SHAPE medians are 0.009 at A and 0.925 at U, a skew that any reported correlation must be corrected for.
pitch.who_wants_it: The Pyle lab (Yale), who built this data and design structure-targeting antisense oligos, and the Das lab / Eterna community, who would learn whether RibonanzaNet needs in-cell training data.

ml_idea: Zero-shot benchmark rather than a training project: run RibonanzaNet (open weights, trained on ~2 million short RNA sequences probed with the same 2A3 and dimethyl sulfate reagents) in sliding windows over the 7,382-nucleotide murine norovirus CW3 genome and compare its predictions with the measured in-cell reactivities, against two baselines I already computed - a per-base median dummy and the replicate noise ceiling (Pearson r = 0.970). Report how accuracy varies by genome region, local structure and sequencing depth. The project only becomes a real paper when pooled with five or more other published in-cell viral probing datasets (SARS-CoV-2, HIV-1, dengue) so that held-out-genome splits exist.

effort.compute_note: Measured, not guessed: the whole deposit is 1.9 MB, all four profiles parse in seconds with pandas, and I already built and queried the merged nucleotide table. Inference cost is estimated at roughly 30-60 windows of a few hundred nucleotides through a small transformer on CPU; nothing was timed for the model itself.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the independent RNA molecules carrying a label. The answer is one (7,382 nucleotides of a single murine norovirus CW3 genome, verified), so there is no group to hold out and nothing to train - do this count before anything else.

verdict_reason: The files are genuinely excellent and everything in Part A passes on inspection: one clean 7,382-row table per replicate, the label already a column, a direct chemical measurement, replicate agreement of 0.970, documented columns, 1.9 MB total, and two positive controls that already pass. The project dies on sample size in disguise: 7,313 labelled rows are 7,313 positions on a single genome from one cell line, so there is no leakage-free split (E1 and E2 both fail) and nothing to train a head on, while RibonanzaNet already exists with open weights trained on the same two reagents across roughly two million sequences. Park it as an external-validation genome: if someone assembles in-cell probing data for five or more viruses so that held-out-genome splits exist, this is a high-quality member of that benchmark, and the useful single-genome result meanwhile is a short note on how far a sequence-only predictor gets beyond knowing the base identity.
